easy
matter.
A study of our Archives reveals a
different story, a
fascinating one, of
a
struggle through the years, from
1850 down, almost a full century, to
the present. It reveals numerous
brave attempts by devoted under
graduates and alumni to found a
peri
odical to record the achievements of
Psi Upsilon. It is a
story of remark
able persistence�even when inter
rupted by failures. Success finally
was achieved.
The earliest printed periodical of
Psi Upsilon, it is believed, was The
College Tablet, "Pubhshed by the
Delta Chapter of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity," and edited by F. N. Za
briskie '50 and E. C. Darlington '50.
The first number was dated January
15, 1850. There were six issues of
eight printed pages, 6x9 inches.
The entire first number was
repro
duced in The Diamond of January
1931.
Early long hand records indicate
that consideration of a
periodical for
the Fraternity, as a whole, first oc
curred at the Convention of 1851�
only 18 years after our
founding. At
this convention, a committee sub
mitted a memorial and its report and
recommendation was as follows :

the most pleasing gratification and pride

brothers, both graduates and students, con
tinue to regard the weffare and prosperity
of our loved Fratemity and as a means of
promoting that interest in a
degree beg

As a
thing calculated to advance in every

tered as
they are
through the length and

glorious causeas a

limits of our chapters, it is proposed to

The committee to whom was re
ferred the memorial respectfully pre

REPORT
The estabhshment of the magazine of the

per

magazine
can be sustained for years,�unless there is

of the Fratemity, we
say we deem it inex

character of the proposed magazine.
The character of the proposed magazine

Psi UpsUonism makes a man narrow, selfish,

The cost of printing 1000 copies of the

one
year, with printed covers and placed

J. C. MUler (Psi)

The report of the committee was accepted,

At the Convention of 1852, held

Some fourteen years later, the
Convention of 1865 considered the

pubhshed. In

Gamma, Zeta, Lambda, Kappa, Psi,
Xi, Alpha, Upsilon, Iota, Phi, Omega,
Pi and Chi. Chapter houses as we
now know them were not in exist
ence.
Telegraphy was only 34 years
old; telephones were two years old;

In the Record of the Convention

It is expected that the Hon. F. M.

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
lard Fiske, Psi '51, of the faculty at
Cornell was a
guiding hand in the
estabhshment of the first Diamond.
The history of the fraternity from
1847 until his death in 1904 is filled
with evidences of Brother Fiske's
contributions to Psi Upsilon. It was
natural for him to be interested in
Brother Bacon's pioneering work on
a
fraternity journal.
Our archives contain a letter writ
ten in longhand by Brother Fiske on
Febraary 22, 1878 to an
Omega
brother regarding the establishment
and sponsorship of this first Dia
mond. His reasons for behoving in
the new Diamond are still current
reasons for its existence today!
Mr. Bacon informs me that the Omega
feels adverse to The Diamond, and wishes
me to mention the matter. It is hardly
fair to condemn the journal when but a
single number has been issued. The thing
is totally new, being the first publication
ever issued devoted purely to the interests
of a Greek Letter Society�the periodicals
started from time to time by other G. L.
organizations having been merely hterary.
Some mistakes will unavoidably be made
in the first issue or two. A portion of the
Fratemity news, too, was
probably of a
nature which should have precluded its in
sertion.
When Mr. Bacon consulted me about
his proposed publication it seemed to me
that the reasons for its existence were over
whelming. The chief ones are as foUows :
1. It ought to form a new and needed
link between graduates and undergradu
ates. The comparatively httle interest taken
by Psi Upsilon graduates in the affairs of
the Fratemity is a
strong electioneering
argument against the organization in our
Eastem colleges. There were conventions
between 1869 and 1875 at which not haff
a dozen graduates were
present. It is true
that this condition of things has been some
what improved by the revival of the Pubhc
Literary Exercises at the Conventions, but
it is StiU true that there is not apparent
among our
graduates that healthy feeling
of interest which characterizes those of
some similar associations. My experience
with the preparation of the catalogue long
ago convinced me that this state of things
is largely owing to lack of information
conceming the condition and growth of
the Fratemity. The Diamond wiff do much
to help do away with their seeming indif
ference, so detrunental to the Chapters
themselves. It has already done much. The
first number was sent to nearly 130 mem
bers of the Theta, graduates prior to 1866;
of these 36 have thus far subscribed with
many words of commendation.
2. Such a
journal ought to be of use in
drawing closer the bond between the
Chapters, which now know httle of each
other. We all know that the officer for
correspondence, owing probably to the
large number of chapters, do not com
municate to other branches of the Frater
nity many matters of interest. The cor
respondence is, in fact, absurdly barren of
information. Even without disclosing what
ought to be kept quiet, much good can be
effected by giving the Chapters some
knowledge of each other.
3. There is in existence ( at the Chi and
elsewhere ) many documents, recorded rem
iniscences, etc., which in no wise cast any
light upon the internal machinery and
working of the Fratemity, but which are
of great interest, and which are known to
very few of our members. Many of these
can
only reach the Fratemity through some
such medium as The Diamond. Such a
document is the "Pledge" of the Founders,
which appears in the February issue. I
have never met an vmdergraduate who
dreamed of the existence of such a
paperthe initial document of our history.
Among those who have expressed the
warmest interest in The Diamond (some
of them offering hberal contributions to
ward its support) are Gov. Rice, Gov.
Hawley, U. S. CoUector Arthur of N. Y.
City, Mr. Ex-Congressman Pettit of In
diana, Judge Hav^ey, Judge Van Vorst
of N. Y. City, Mr. Ex-Congressman W. E.
Robinson (Founder of die Beta), Ex.
U. S. Senator Patiierson and many other
prominent members. A revival of Frater
nity interest among such men as these can
not but produce most important results.
Mr. Bacon informed me that the great
est possible care vnll be taken in the man
agement of the joumal. No documents will
be pubhshed which possess any other im
portance than merely a historical one, and,
in general, no
chapter ever wiU be in
serted except such as is contributed by the
chapters themselves or the CouncU. Mr.
Bacon did not enter upon the enterpnse
without carefuUy consulting many gradu690

ates and undergraduates. After all, it is an

PSI U.
Dear Sir and Brother:
Just now the PSI UPSILON seems to be

ness and prosperity. The Chapters are un

Many have built or are

But what is perhaps more signfficant than
aU this is the fact that many distinguished
graduates�mindful of their vows and re
caUing the pleasant memories of Psi U�
have recently shovim, in various ways, a

hood.
Under these favorable circumstances it

the publication of a
monthly joumal de
signed to aid this general progressive move

joumal was accordingly be

THE DIAMOND. The venture was not

THE DIAMOND is the first joumal ever
issued exclusively devoted to me interests
of a Greek Letter Fratemity, and the first,
the avowed aim of which is to elevate the
student-hfe of America. To place it beyond

sired to do more than meet the absolutely
necessary expenses) a few more subscrip
tions are
necessary, and yours is respect
fuUy solicited.
Yours in the fratemal bonds of Psi
Upsilon,
CHARLES PUTNAM BACON,
Lock Box 11,
Ithaca, New York.

Through these years, from 1878 on,

The Conventions and the Council
